utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber was informed that there were problems, technical problems with our recording system, so that's why we are starting a little late. Good afternoon, Doctor. Can we continue, Mr. Pantelic, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm ready.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Pantelic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Dr. Stanimirovic.

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You may begin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I hope you had a good rest over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the circumstances, let's say that I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we adjourned on Friday and finished our work on that day, you spoke about your work in the local clinic in Donja Slatina. You described how the wounded were treated. You mentioned that there were killed people and generally described the atmosphere that prevailed there practically at the front line. In this context, I wanted to ask you, since you spoke that most of the wounded and the killed were Serbs, although there were other members of other ethnicities, can you tell us: The wounded and the killed at the front line, were those young men, young soldiers, were from originally?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assistance that we rendered at this clinic mainly was administered to the local population of Donja Slatina, Batkusa, and maybe the general area of these two villages. And there were a few people from Samac as well. That accounted for the majority of my patients there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Among your patients in that period in Donja Slatina, were there any civilians? Were they also victims of injuries and war operations?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were. There were injured civilians and there were few cases of civilians who were dead on arrival. At the clinic, mostly as a result of shelling or a stray bullet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since we tackled this subject, the medical service in Samac, how did they establish a death? Can you explain us briefly the medical procedure?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time while I was in Slatina, the medical centre operated at the head of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The interpreter didn't get the name of the director of the clinic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can the witness repeat the name of the head of the centre?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The interpreter failed to hear the name. Can you please go back?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Mesud Nogic. He was the head of the medical centre and he was a gynaecologist by profession. The standard procedure was applied in such cases, as always. When there are definite signs of death, the person is proclaimed death [sic].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Dr. Stanimirovic, tell me, please: How did you get medical supplies at the clinic where you worked, and generally, if you know, how the medical service functioned at that period in the territory of Samac municipality? Was it military service or civilian service? How did it work?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I worked in the civilian clinic, I relied on the medical centre, and that is a civilian institution. I told you that before the war a huge quantity of medical supplies and medicines had arrived, so that I provided these for my clinic where I worked from the medical centre. Since at the time in Samac my wife and my friends lived in Samac, I very frequently took the advantage of that and used to go there to collect the medical supplies and to visit my family at the same time. Since I lived in the village, and I also took these opportunities to take some food to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the occasions that you visited your family in Samac, what did you notice about the town? Were there any combat operations? Was there any shelling? Can you describe the atmosphere in the town?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I went to visit, there wasn't any such things, because I didn't stay longer than half an hour, because my clinic didn't have any other doctor, and I usually had difficulties to get the permission to go to town, because I had to claim that I was short of bandages, otherwise they wouldn't let me go. So I couldn't stay for a long time, and during the half hour that I usually spent in the town, there was no shelling. That -- I'm talking about the first four months, and during that period, whenever I went there, there was no shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice how the buildings looked like? Did you talk to the members of your family? Did they report to you, perhaps, about -- on the situation?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were shellings, and even the apartment block where I lived was hit several times. But I was fortunate enough that whenever time -- whenever I went there in those first few months, this did not happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you spoke earlier about a huge quantity of medical supplies which surprised you as something unusual, before the conflicts broke out, do you have any information where these supplies had come from? Do you have this kind of information?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the stories told around the medical centre, these supplies had arrived from Germany.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you discuss with your family the atmosphere related to the supply for the civilian population with food supplies and the activities of the Red Cross? You mentioned that you were active in the Red Cross for many years. Can you tell us: When you went to Samac on occasion, at times, how the supply provisions of staples and basic provisions functioned for the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My wife is a diabetic, and I always had problems with her diet, and a few things that I had brought with me cannot apply to the rest of the population. Since the clinic where I worked was in a village, the local population lives on producing vegetables for the market, I got a lot of these vegetables for free, because they were not able to sell it on the market, and I brought this vegetables to the building where I lived, distributed it to my neighbours or to my friends who came to visit me at my place. However, I cannot say what the situation was in the stores and shops, because I didn't have time to go around and look, and I didn't have time to discuss this with my wife, because I was always in a hurry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Stanimirovic, tell me: Since -- in view of your enviable length of service in the medical profession, at the time, did you get any information from your colleagues from the Red Cross, whether the Red Cross had undertaken any measures to provide food and other necessities for the population? If you know.

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the time that I spent in Donja Slatina, I cannot say, but when I returned from Donja Slatina, took over the management over the medical centre, of course I contacted the Red Cross, because at the time I was member of the presidency of the Red Cross organisation. And we organised campaigns for blood donations, and I am also myself a blood donor. And naturally, I could influence, to the best of my abilities, how these things were distributed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that your colleague, Dr. Nogic, and you mentioned that on Friday, was appointed coordinator or the director of all medical services. Tell me: What was your relationship with Dr. Nogic and your cooperation while you worked in Donja Slatina? How would you characterise that?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was my superior, according to the hierarchy. He was a director. But basically, we always had good cooperation, because we are personal friends. For some time, we studied together, although he was older than me. But we met at the university. So we go a long way back. He's an old friend of mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were running this local clinic in Donja Slatina, did you have contacts with Dr. Nogic along the professional lines?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Whenever I went to collect some material, I always got in touch with him, not only with him, but with other colleagues as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Between April and August of 1992, while you worked in the place that you just described, tell me: In your contacts with Dr. Nogic, did he complain about he was being treated, in view of the fact that he was a Muslim, did he make any statements to that effect?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, he didn't complain to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You already mentioned that the ethnic composition of the medical service in the year 1992 was a mixed one. When you went to Samac, to the headquarters of the medical service, did any of your non-Serb colleagues complain to you personally about how they were treated or of the status that they enjoyed?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, they didn't to me, but even if anyone had wanted to complain, they didn't have time for that. I stayed for a very short time. I took what I wanted to take with me and I went back to my clinic. This clinic was very busy and one could never know when a wounded man, person, would be brought in, and it wouldn't be good for someone -- for a patient to die in my absence. That is why I was always in such a great hurry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Dr. Stanimirovic: When you took over the post of the coordinator of the medical centre, after you had been working in Donja Slatina, what particularly was your duty? How did you organise the medical service and these kind of services in Samac? That took place sometime in September, in I'm correct.

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In late September or beginning of October, when I came there, there were five or six colleagues of mine, and I was looking forward to some good time of rest. I would be working no more than four or five hours [as interpreted]. We had a lot of equipment and medical supplies, so we had -- we didn't have this kind of problems. And the service was organised in such a manner --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you for a second, please. Maybe the interpreters didn't hear well. Did you work shifts four or five hours or longer?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said the shifts were 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We organised it at the level of emergency service, because in the morning there were always three or four of us, and over the night, one or two of us were always there. However, one of our colleagues was always in charge of the shift. As soon as one of the colleagues would leave Samac, we had to intensify or extend our shifts, and sometime in 1993 it happened that I had 20 shifts a month, whereas the remaining ten days I worked only the morning shift, that is, 12 hours during the daylight. Because there were no more than three doctors in the medical centre. Dr. Joka Savic, a microbiologist; Dr. Ruzmir Jusufovic, a pediatrician and internal medicine specialist; and myself. Since we had two locations where we had to work, that is, hospital with a dialysis ward and internal medicine ward, I assigned Dr. Ruzmir Jusufovic to cover that ward, and Dr. Joka and I worked both in the hospital and in the medical centre. Then a female colleague of ours came, so we released Dr. Ruzmir his night shifts, since he was already in charge of the chemo-dialysis and the internal medicine ward and the three of us divided between ourselves 60 shifts. Each had 20 shifts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Ruzmir is of what ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you managed the medical service, can you tell us, according to the establishment, how did it function? What did this Samac local medical service cover? What kind of institutions did you cover?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had medical centre, hospital with chemo-dialysis and I had sector clinics. In some of the sector clinics, just like the sector clinic of Obudovac, I had a colleague who worked permanently there. Then the sector clinic, Gornja Slatina, also one doctor on a permanent basis, sector clinic Donja Slatina, which I had left before that, also had a permanent doctor employed there. And the other sector clinics that we covered in Odzak, Novi Grad, Dubica, Kruskovo Polje, doctors came occasionally, once or twice a week, as necessary. Then we set up a clinic in Lipik, a village by the name of Lipik, and we went there once a week. As part of this operation, this was towards the end of 1993 and early 1994, when the combat operations were not as frequent as they had been, some of our colleagues had returned, namely, so that we could manage better, so that already at the beginning of 1993, we organised -- rather, I tried to organise us to resemble a civilian service as much as possible in peacetime conditions. Now, that implies that meant that I had actually set up a number of infirmaries, such as the gynaecological ward, with Dr. Nogic in charge; the pediatrics ward, with Dr. Rusmir in charge, the tuberculosis infirmary, with myself in charge; and I also set up a vaccination service for the inoculation of children. I myself actually was not quite certain that this would indeed function. However, it did, and it functioned quite well, so that already by 1993 we had carried out the necessary vaccinations of all the children in the municipality, according to their actual need. And interestingly enough, at that time we did not have the necessary vaccines, so we had to purchase them in Belgrade and bring them in clandestinely, as it were, and then we proceeded to vaccinate the children in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When it comes to the organising of the medical service and all the necessary -- supplying all the necessary medical supplies, the equipment for work to be as regular as possible of the medical service in Samac, can you describe to us your relationship with the -- as the manager of the clinic with the leadership of the municipality of Samac at the time?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, I did not exactly knock on the municipal doors to beg for help. Fortunately, Dr. Simic, when he came there to work with us as a young colleague, and I was some kind of a mentor to him, I explained to him what my idea was as to how this service was to be organised and I was given full support for this exercise. So that whenever I needed anything, I could call him, and I would be given what I needed. In fact, for the first time, the first time for these vaccines, when we got these vaccines, he was the one who gave me the money. It is from him that I also received the monies for the dialysis, which was an enormous problem at the time, because we had no electricity. We had no electric power at the time. We did have a very big generator to generate energy. This was a specific tailor-made dialysis centre. It was a very modern one. But unfortunately, without oil, it could not operate. So that we also obtained the necessary oil in a similar fashion, as also the necessary money for the equipment, various needles, intravenous equipment. Let me not bore you with all that. But we needed the money and all these things had to be purchased. This is where we enjoyed the absolute support of the municipal authorities. The only problem was how to find these things in Belgrade, how to get them there, how to buy them and bring them. The money was no object.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please tell me of what nationality were the patients who were treated in the medical centre in Samac while you were in charge of it?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, ours is a mixed community, so in the town of Samac itself, there lived Muslims, Serbs, and Croats. The Muslims are, in principle, the founders of the city of Samac, in the modern, in the more modern sense of the word, and the surrounding villages are Serb and Croat villages. There is not a single Muslim village. So that the patients who -- that we attended to were of all these three nations. We extended assistance to all patients, to all of them, irrespective of their ethnicity or their sex or any other characteristic, because every doctor who was employed there could actually make his own autonomous decisions and could attend to whatever patient he wanted to. As for me, as the head of this service, I have no information that anyone has not been given adequate treatment at any time during that time. Namely, what I'm saying is that no patient complained to me of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Has anyone from the civilian authorities during this time when you were head of this clinic exerted any pressure on you or your colleague in the sense that no medical assistance should be extended to any person who is a non-Serb? Were there any pressures of that kind?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I object. Very leading. There are other ways he can ask that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic. You can rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I will rephrase that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell me: Have the civilian authorities -- did the civilian authorities have any contacts with you personally in respect to certain criteria when it came to the treatment of patients, in terms of their ethnicity or anything similar? Do you have any information to that effect?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No such thing happened, for the simple reason because I mainly contacted and liaised with Dr. Simic, because he himself is a physician. As regards the rest of the people in the leadership of the municipality then, I did not have any need to actually liaise with them, because this is not a subject that they are versed in. And I enjoyed a very valuable support of this colleague of mine, so that I had a free hand, as it were, and could do, together with my colleague, what we thought was best.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that it was very difficult to organise the chemo-dialysis service, which is a very, very specialised intervention, a delicate one. Can you describe for us everything that you did for this chemo-dialysis service to function during the war in the municipality of Samac, generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Samac is an endemic area of nephropathy, meaning that we have very many, many people affected with nephropathy. So everything that could be done in fact I believe that we paid more attention to dialysis than to any other branches of medicine. And, you know, if this equipment and -- did not operate for seven days, that would mean five to ten people would die, at least. And that would indeed be a great blow to the medical service there. So that we did our best for that particular ward to function, which meant that we had, A, to procure the necessary oil, that we had to also make available, purchase, procure, all the necessary supporting supplies, the dilutions for chemo-dialysis, for instance there was the shortage of heparin, heparin, which is a liquid which prevents blood from clotting, coagulating, so we would be without that particular medicine. We would spend money and go and get it elsewhere. So we actually made do and we did not have any emergencies in that particular respect. Sometimes towards the end of our work on this chemo-dialysis, when the international community actually stepped in and promised to help us with the dialysis, we actually contemplated the idea of confining the dialysis to just once a week, whereas the standard, the normal requirement is three to four a week. Fortunately, we managed to maintain the level at two dialyses a week, and then the international humanitarian organisation stepped in and helped us so that we could continue regular operation in that sense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you any information to the effect whether the civilian authorities had set up any commission to travel outside Samac in order to procure the necessary medical supplies for dialysis, for this to technically function?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The colleague who was in charge of dialysis, before our colleague Ruzmir was Mirko Sisic. He was an internal medicine specialist. And he was doing his master's thesis at that time. So it actually suited him to travel quite frequently to Belgrade. And it was very convenient, a convenient excuse to him to go and say, "Look, I'm going to go and get the supplies necessary for dialysis, so on one of those trips, actually, our car got stolen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that during the war period everything possible had been done in order to secure the necessary salaries for the medical staff. Can you tell me what the economic situation was like in the period between 1992 and 1994?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The economic situation was very difficult. People who had some savings had some money. But for a while, even those who had money could not purchase anything. The population of the cities had nothing to buy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no green markets where you could buy, for instance, potatoes, beans, or onions. Fortunately most of our population was of a rural origin, so they somehow made do, managed to survive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what the inflation rate was?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember it was a horrific inflation rate. I could not pay out the salaries to the staff of the medical centre because the paper, the explanation for that which I gave them was that the paper which the accountant used to write out the pay slips actually cost me more than the money that we would be actually giving people as salaries, and that salary could not buy you a box of matches. And I thought that was indeed offensive, so I wouldn't pay out the people's salaries. And I explained it to them, and the employees actually agreed to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under these circumstances which you have just described, were there any other ways of recompensing the people in any other forms in lieu of their salaries?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, of course there were. There were people working in the medical centre who lived in the city, who had neither friends nor relations in the country, in the villages, and could not obtain the necessary food from the villages. So that we organised this campaign for them to be given parcels of food. On other occasions we would organise something like call it exactly -- I cannot call it exactly a salary, but this was more in the way of relief assistance, sanitary parcels, hygienic kits and the like for people who had no relations in the village who would provide them with such things. And in principle I saw to it that this was taken care of properly for such people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the period when you started working as the head and coordinator of the medical service, did you have any contacts with Stevan Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, when I arrived in Samac, I had, for instance, in the prison there was no medical care, if you will, or supervision. So I went to see him so as to arrange for this to be organised, and I thought that this was my duty and obligation as a physician. Well, this did not actually go smoothly, but since I myself am not a man who gives in easily, I explained to the chief of police that many people in one place devoid of medical care and without proper hygienic conditions actually constituted a potential source of infection and that their guards in the prison would be the first ones to be infected and that eventually the chief of police would himself get the infection. So I was given permission to organise, set up an infirmary there, which I did, and I also supervised the maintenance of hygiene there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who gave you this permission?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did that function in practice?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once or twice a week I would go there, report to the policeman there, who would then take me into the prison, which was not a real prison, but it was the prison then. And then he would take me into one of the rooms, and everyone who was sick then could come and see me, to be examined. I had with me a small quantity of the necessary medicines, mainly painkillers and analgesics, antibiotics, and some tranquilisers sometimes. So I maintained the record of the ill. And once I finished that, I would then proceed to my next job. So I had such infirmaries in the prison in Samac, which was across from the SUP, the secretariat of the interior, and I also had a similar infirmary in the inner village, which is called Zasavica. There I was given a house, or rather, a room in a house, where I set up this clinic, this infirmary, and I was assisted there by the people who were isolated, as they put it then, because this was not a real prison; it was an isolation situation. There's also an old schoolmate, high schoolmate there, and he was my orderly, or nurse. And when he left, different people did the job, mainly people, persons whom I already knew personally and could trust and could really feel at ease doing my work. If I needed dental service, the services of a dentist, I would either write them a slip or I would take them in an ambulance car, and the same went when it came to laboratory services. Once that was over, they would then return.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, doctor: You mentioned this infirmary which you had set up in the Detention Unit, shall we call it, across the street from the SUP, which building was that?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Samac, we call it the TO, Territorial Defence building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: What are your observations in the period when you were extending such medical services? What are your observations about the medical situation, status, of the patients?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw anyone officially beaten. What I did see on one occasion was a fractured hand or arm. It is hard to explain this fractured arm which I mobilised immediately. That was no problem at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Officially beaten. I mean he said something like he was beaten recently or something like that would more accurate translation than officially beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. We heard in our earphones kind of freshly, but I will clarify that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please repeat your answer? What were your observations about the medical status of the patients when you treated them there? But slowly, please, Dr. Stanimirovic, for -- because I have noticed that you are sometimes unintelligible. So please slow down.

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never noticed any fresh traces, recent traces of violent injury on any patients that reported to me, to be examined by me in that infirmary. I saw fractured arm. It was a closed fracture. I did not see any injuries to tissue above the fracture. And when I asked the patient how the fracture had occurred, he told me that he had taken a fall, which is a quite probable, a quite possible --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry. The interpreter corrects herself --

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- cause. But I did laugh because this possible cause is a relative thing in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please tell me: What was the extent of your professional services concretely in this TO building? Will you explain whether you needed to transfer the detainees, for instance, to hospital for some surgical operations or anything of the kind. Please be so kind as to explain to us the level of medical services required by the patients.

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the illnesses that occurred there were at the level of the general practitioner's medical assistant. So there was no need for sending them further on. For example, there was not a single case of appendicitis, which is an acute surgical matter that requires an operation. And such-like illnesses we did not have. And I was not forced to use my personal influence to have some of the patients transferred to hospital. Had it been necessary, I don't think that would have been a problem. But as I said, I believe, since I didn't have a chance to test this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Dr. Stanimirovic: For how long did this infirmary operate, and what was the reason for it to stop, if it stopped operating? Can you explain?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both in the TO prison and in Zasavica, worked there to meet the needs of the people who were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to say for how long. Perhaps I worked there for two months. I have problems with dates, because at the time every day, even every month, was all the same to me. And those people were transported to other institutions and transferred to other institutions and there was no need for me to run this infirmary any more. And therefore, the infirmary was closed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any personal knowledge about where those people -- the detainees from the TO building were transferred?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me: In connection with Zasavica, what kind of -- you said that was a village. Tell us: Were there any fences, wires, guards, any armed force there? Can you describe the situation in Zasavica? Because that is also where you rendered medical services.

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the entrance to the village that I had to pass through, there were policemen, and they had their checkpoint there, in a building that was in fact a tavern before the war, owned by a friend of mine and where I frequently went. So whenever I came, I had to stop by, only this time to report to the police and pass through, also on the way back I passed through, waved my hand at them. If I wrote a recommendation that a dentist services were necessary or laboratory services were necessary, my patient would come there as well with this written recommendation of mine. They would record this, and whenever he returned, his return was recorded again. There was no wire, wired fence, but as I said, there was police at the entrance of the village. I even think that there are two entrance points, in fact, there's an entrance and an exit point to the village. And that on the other side the police was there occasionally, but I didn't go in that direction, so I cannot say for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any personal knowledge why this police checkpoint was set up there?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I had been told, because I couldn't help asking them what they were doing there, they told me that they were guarding the people in the village so as that no one would come from outside to maltreat them, and that was all I had ever asked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: How would you describe the work of this infirmary in Zasavica? What was the scope of your work? What kind of cases did you treat? What services did you offer, in medical terms? Can you give us a few details?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was also at the level of the general practice. I knew all of those people, and I knew that there were some people with low blood pressure, pneumatic ailments, and things like that. And it was very strange that those people came now more rarely and had less medical problems, health problems, than before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How come?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably, before the war we had a very comfortable medical service, and if you don't have anything better to do in your life, you take your social medical security card, you go to the medical centre, and you can request whatever you wanted, and that was all for free. The second thing which also was one of the reasons: People became serious and started taking care of themselves, because at that time you couldn't eat as much as you wanted: Fat food, salty food, even they were running out of cigarettes. So when people started leading a healthier life, more healthy life, it became obvious in their medical records.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, generally, what was the situation with the food supplies in Zasavica? Were there any farms in Zasavica? Did they grow any vegetables? Can you describe that, please? What kind of village was that?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was an agricultural village living on agriculture. They grew and had always grown vegetables and fruit. In Posavina, where we live, the soil is very good, fertile, and I noticed that people bred hogs as well, a large number of hogs, and I was interested in that and asked them what was that all about. They told me that that was a hog farm for human nutrition, consumption.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that medical service was organised in various villages, including Odzak. Can you tell us more about that? How was that organised? Was Odzak a place where anyone can walk in freely or was there another arrangement?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Odzak was, so to say, under the military government. I think that the Samac Brigade was in charge there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please repeat, because there was a misinterpretation. What did you say about Samac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I went to Odzak, I had a special pass which I obtained in Odzak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please repeat your previous sentence when you mentioned the Samac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Samac Brigade was not in charge of Odzak, because I had to request another military pass to be issued to me, and I got it from another unit. Although I had also the pass issued by the Samac Brigade, which allowed me to move around Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how did the medical service function in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went there once a week, and if there was not much work, I asked a colleague who worked in this Krajina unit --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear what the counsel said. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, can you remember pausing. The witness's answer wasn't given completely when you started asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I try, Your Honour, to advise him to speak a little bit slower for the interpreters, because I saw that from time to time it's very hard to catch what the witness has said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Dr. Stanimirovic, kindly, could you please speak a little bit more slowly so that we have a proper record and avoid misunderstandings. So let me repeat the question. How did the medical service in Odzak function? You said that you went there once a week if there was not much to do, when there was not much to do, that they would ask a colleague of yours to substitute for you, and this colleague worked for a Krajina unit. Can you continue from there, but slowly.

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since this unit was not sufficiently supplied with medicines, I used to leave to this colleague of mine a certain quantity of some basic medicaments to distribute them to civilians, who would come to them -- to him, and I asked him to see those people. And that is how it worked in Odzak. In Novi Grad, in the infirmary there, which was located in the veterinarian station, we had a nurse working there on a permanent basis. So there were no problems with the functioning there, because she was an experienced nurse. So in my absence, she was able to issue medicines according to the medical -- patient's medical record or the protocol, where I had put in the proper -- the necessary treatment. There was another infirmary in Donja Dubica, and Lipik as well, but they were infirmaries of lesser significance, so it's not necessary to discuss them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of services were rendered there, or what were the most often ailments of your patients there?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were mainly elderly people, returnees, and one might have expected to see there cases of rheumatism, high blood pressure, and heart conditions. And generally speaking, all of them requested tranquilisers to be prescribed to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that the patients in this area were returnees. Where had they returned from? What nationality were they? And basically, how did it happen that they returned to Odzak in the first place? What do you know about that personally?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, some of them fled Odzak or Novi Grad or whatnot but some did not manage to escape, and they got captured.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What nationality were they?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were Serbs. And when the situation on the ground changed, they returned, and that is how they became my patients.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now I would like to comment with you a number of documents that have been admitted here as exhibits. Can you comment on them briefly, if you have any personal knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I would like to -- Exhibit D109/1 to be shown to the witness, please. Mr. Usher, please, on the ELMO, please, because of the other participants in the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you mind, Mr. Stanimirovic, just to look at this exhibit and then return it so that we can all have a look.

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Take it, look at it carefully, and then return it back so that we all can see it.

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, this was signed by Dr. Sisic. There's no need for me to look at it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Give us your comment what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Properly, since Dr. Sisic was head of the dialysis ward at the time, and he is a very responsible person, what he has written here must be right and correct. I have confidence in the colleagues that I used to work with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Usher. Could we have now Exhibit D118/1, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You first look at it carefully. Don't be hasty. Thank you. Tell me, Dr. Stanimirovic: Since we are looking at the end of 1992 and later on we shall discuss this document, but before that, tell me: Do you have any personal knowledge about possible number of refugees in Samac municipality at that time? Approximately, do you know? If you don't, just tell me you don't remember.

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to say. I can say in general terms, but I cannot divide it by months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the end of 1992?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to say. I had just arrived in Samac, and I cannot remember seeing this kind of paper, but I do remember that I was in - how was it called - something for natural disasters. Yes, civilian protection. I was a member of the civilian protection in my capacity of medical doctor, and most probably this is the result of that function.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Usher. Can we have now Exhibit D103/1, please. Mr. Usher, can I just check this document? Yes. It's -- it's number D, so I need 103A/1. It's my mistake. Sorry. Because this document consist of -- this exhibit consist of several documents. I think it's pay list of the pharmacy. It should be first one. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you take a look at the names, Dr. Stanimirovic, please, on this list. Will you tell us whether you know these people?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please put that on the ELMO so that everyone can see. This is the May 1992 payroll. It's a very clear document. Tell me about these people, Mrs. Almasa Hadzialijagic. Do you know this piece?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jusufovic, Almasa, she was a pharmacist, master of pharmacy, as we say. Of course I know her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is her nationality?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She is a Muslim, and she helped me a lot during the war. She was in charge of our pharmacy and was so impeccable in performing her duty that I could actually boast about the work of that particular pharmacy when we were taken over by the International Red Cross. And when they started donating us the medicines we needed. All the medicaments from such donations actually went to this particular pharmacy. And Mrs. Almasa kept the records in the pharmacy and she maintained records on every individual pill, which means that whenever you wanted to undertake any control of the medicines which you had given me, or to the medical centre, conditionally speaking, I would then take you to this pharmacy and I would tell you. This medicine is either on the shelf or has been issued to a patient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, will you please lead the witness to give us evidence which is relevant. We don't need these details. It's a waste of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'll take care of it. Thank you, Mr. Usher. Just leave the exhibit here and I will briefly discuss the matter with the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please tell me, sir, Dr. Stanimirovic: During the war, where was Mrs. Almasa?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was the head of the pharmacy throughout that period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any information as to her current whereabouts?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She is still working in the pharmacy, but she is not the chief of the pharmacy, the head of the pharmacy. While I was there, she always was the head of the pharmacy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As regards the other workers on this list, can you give us any information as to their ethnicity, if you know, of course?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zorka Hadzialijagic is a Serbian lady married to a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry. Sorry. I cannot follow. Please ask the witness to slow down. The interpreter cannot follow the --

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last one, I am not sure whether she is a Serbian or a Croatian lady.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please slow down, because the interpreters cannot manage to catch up with you. Would you please repeat the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I was going to ask him to repeat, because he was speaking a lot, but there was no translation. It just didn't pick up whatever he was saying, they didn't pick up whatever he was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So for the needs of the record and to assist our interpreters, would you please slow down a bit. Of course, it is easy for us to understand each other, speaking the same language as we are, but for the record and for everybody else, we need a clear record. Please, Dr. Stanimirovic, would you please kindly repeat, if you know, from among the people on this payroll list. You have already referred to the ethnicity of Mrs. Jusufovic Almasa, so please slowly repeat us, if you have information about the national -- the ethnicity of the other people work in the pharmacy.

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zorka Hadzialijagic, a Serbian lady married to a Muslim man; Rasida Drljacic, a Muslim lady; Ruza Popovic, a Serb lady; Jovanka Petrovic, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Another question regarding this particular subject. Tell me, Dr. Stanimirovic: What contacts, if any, did you have with members of the International Red Cross? Would you please describe the relationship which you had with them.

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My contacts with International Red Cross were exceptionally good. This was so especially when they witnessed for themselves how we distributed the medicaments which they gave me. In fact, they even commended the operation of the pharmacy, our pharmacy, because of its operation and the way in which it operated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, but in order for this evidence to make any sense, could he give us some sort of time period that he's talking about? Is this 1993, 1994? When is this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It is just -- proper question. I was just about to ask the witness about the time frame. I'm grateful to my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Stanimirovic, would you please tell me the period from the fall of 1992, when you assumed the leadership and the post of coordinator of the medical services until the end of 1993, this is the period that we're interested in relevant to the indictment, did you have in that period any contacts with the Red Cross? What was the relationship like and what were the conclusions like of your mutual contacts, if any? So we're interested in that particular period only, nothing later interests us.

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that we had such contacts also during 1993, even though it is very hard for me to set a time frame to determine the actual year, but the mechanism of the distribution of relief supplies was the way I've described it from the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether there have been any other subjects that you discussed in the period in question with the representatives of the International Red Cross, apart from the distribution of medicaments? Did you talk about the quality of the medical services, medical care offered to the population or any other subject in that domain?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people who came to talk to us on behalf of the Red Cross from Geneva were mainly secondary-level-education people, so that I did not discuss specific treatment options with them. But we did talk about the need to supply Samac with medicaments, and I always tried to obtain vaccines, insulin, and also drugs for the treatment of psychiatric patients.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Dr. Stanimirovic, from which sources did these drugs come to Samac in 1992 and 1993? You referred to one source, which is the International Red Cross. Were there any other lines of supply with medicaments to Samac?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were. We got considerable quantities of medicaments from people who lived and who had lived and lived in our municipality and worked abroad, so that they too collected medicines and sent us such medicines, so that also the Red Cross of Yugoslavia and a number of other humanitarian organisations, the names of which I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to -- well, I have intention to tender into evidence three documents already disclosed to the -- to our friends from Prosecution. Mainly these are the blood donors and the other patients, non-Serb patients treated during the period covered by indictment. So I wonder -- it will take some time. We shall go into the -- our break. So would it be appropriate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We can start now, because the documents are several, as you said. So you can start with the first document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Please, Mr. Usher, could I have your assistance. There are five copies here for the Bench and the two for the registry. The first document is under our internal number R28. This is a list of blood donors dated September 14th of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any objection from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: None at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have the number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D145/1 and ter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Stanimirovic, take a look at this document. You can in fact -- you can in fact look at it during the break, because we will comment on it after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you want me to continue or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take our break and continue proceedings at 1615 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the break, Dr. Stanimirovic, we started discussing this document. It was compiled on the 14th September 1992. And when you look at the list of these blood donors, do you recognise some of names contained therein?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, lots of them. Almost all of them, because I was one of them. And this date helps me to determine when I arrived at Samac. That means after the 14th of September, because otherwise I would have been on this list as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you recognise a number of people on the list.

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before, let me ask you: Are these the residents of Samac?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is their ethnicity? Is that a single ethnicity list of the inhabitants or does it contain -- but you don't have to go one by one. Can you just tell me: How do you assess the ethnic composition here?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a mixed list, and in any case, the blood donors are always of mixed ethnic composition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1992 and 1993, were there more campaigns of this nature or was this the only one?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were more campaigns like this, because it's common knowledge that in a war, where people get wounded, blood is never in sufficient quantities. So that in principle, this kind of campaigns are carried out three or four times a year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, if you know, whether in 1992 and 1993 there were any damage inflicted on the hospital; and if there was, what was the cause and when did it happen? If you know.

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember because lots of artillery missiles fell inside the hospital compound. With this I refer to mortar shells. That's what I had been told, because I'm no expert in this field. And one of these shells hit directly the chemo-dialysis room. The good thing was that at the time there were no patients in the room, because a small number of patients had undergone this dialysis that were positive, as we classified them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have personal knowledge of any possible shelling or bombardment of water supply systems?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On one occasion when I was off duty, I had a free night, I went home. I was sitting at my neighbour's. An agricultural plane appeared, and it tried to hit the water supply system and the post office. However, it missed both the water supply system and the post office, but it broke our windows, because the building where I live is some 150 metres far from the water supply system. Of course, we didn't know immediately what had happened, because we were frightened, and the following day we learned what in fact occurred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The next document which I would like to discuss with this witness is under the internal enumeration R 34. So I believe for this document we already have exhibit number, for the blood donor list, Ms. Registrar --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We were given 145.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have the number for this one, internal number 34.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Our internal number, I said is R 34. I believe I said it. So the next document which I would like to discuss with the witness. Mr. Usher, please, I will provide you with one copy so that you can put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit D146/1 and ter for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could we get a description of that document, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This is a list of new and incumbent non-Serb patients of chemo-dialysis in Samac on 16 April 1992 and who were dialysed during the entire war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Stanimirovic, this is a list that was made in the year 2001, based on the records. Tell me: The signature on this document is presumed of Dr. Nenad Petkovic. Do you know this person?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know colleague Petkovic. He is currently the head of the chemo-dialysis ward. He had taken out this information from the protocol, because at the time he was not involved in the dialysis procedure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I would like to know, since you have personal knowledge about certain number of patients: Can you recall whether these patients that are in the list and who are Muslims and Croats, were they, in 1992 and 1993, being treated by chemo-dialysis in Samac?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were, and this list is authentic. I do not know that a single person had been deprived for any reason the service of chemo-dialysis in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd move to strike --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd move to strike the last part of his answer. The question was whether or not these persons did in fact take chemo -- or receive chemo-dialysis, and that's what we're trying to get at, whether these persons were -- and then he added his own comment about who was -- not a single person was deprived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I will allow that to remain on record, because I don't think the Prosecution's case is -- has anything to do with the deprivation of chemo-dialysis treatment to anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. So it will remain on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The next document which I would like to discuss with this witness is under our internal number R 35 and the title is list of non-Serb patients treated in the department for internal medicine in Samac in the period 16 April 1992 to 31st December 1993. And if there is no objection from the Prosecution, I hope we shall get a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit D147/1 and D147/1 ter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Stanimirovic, take a look at this document. It has two pages. And if you cannot see properly, take a closer look at it so that you can see what it contains. Tell me -- will you please turn to page 2. Is that the signature of your colleague Petkovic, who had signed the previous list as well?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was signed by Dr. Petkovic, the official head of the dialysis ward. I have no objection to this list, because this list has been taken and a copy made from the general record of patients.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your personal knowledge about any individuals in this list? Do you personally know that in the said period they received medical services at the internal medicine ward in Samac?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know many of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's not -- he says he knows many of them. The question was did they receive medical services. That was the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I thought he had a "yes" at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I will try to clarify that with the witness. No problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So Dr. Stanimirovic, let us be accurate. Do you personally know if any or all individuals in the list received medical services in the internal medicine ward? So the question is not whether you know anyone from this list. Instead, I'm asking you: Did they receive medical services in the said period?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The head of the ward at that time was Dr. Sisic, Jerko. He was a highly professional person. And each of these individuals in the list was hospitalised and received medical assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that your personal knowledge?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know colleague Sisic, and after September or October, I was his superior, and I can say that that was correct. If it happens that one of medical doctors wants to hide someone in the hospital, it is quite normal that such person would receive medication and medical assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell me now, in the end, Dr. Stanimirovic, how would you describe Dr. Blagoje Simic as a person? How long have you known him? How would you assess him?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met Dr. Simic after he graduated from the university and came to us to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many years would that be?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many years. Ten years since 1992, and most certainly three or four years before that. So let's say between 13 and 15 years. Because my hobby is to be on duty in the emergency ward, which is a part of the medical centre. I have frequent contacts, both with general practitioners, among whom was Dr. Simic. Since I'm a senior doctor, I made effort to train my younger colleagues, and that is how we became friends. Before the war, we used to -- our practice was that the doctors who were on duty in the emergency ward make a party in my weekend cottage once a month. So we were quite a nice company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how would you characterise or describe Dr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My opinion is that he is very responsible and humane medical doctor. Whenever I had a problem, I turned to Dr. Simic, and he always backed me. When Dr. Simic left, I was also dismissed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Stanimirovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Examination-in-chief of this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Just one small point of clarification. It might be to do with the translation. Page 35, the answer beginning on line 19, Dr. Stanimirovic, talking about his colleague Dr. Sisic, goes on to say, "If it happens that one of the medical doctors wants to hide someone in the hospital, it is quite normal that such person would receive medication and medical assistance." I'm just wondering whether in fact the witness used the word "hide," one of the doctors hiding somebody in the hospital, because your question wasn't related to such an activity. You see what I'm referring to, Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I will clarify that with the -- with Dr. Stanimirovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please explain what this was about?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For instance, I have this friend and he has to go and do something, do -- perform a job, and he doesn't feel like doing it. I can admit him to hospital. I can say that he has pneumonia, open a case file for him, also set up a therapy list for him, put him in bed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: So if I understand correctly, was the hiding of persons going on in the medical institution you were directing; and if so, who was being hidden?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know, all of us, we have a friend -- some friends that we want to help, so that you can put it that way, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stanimirovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any other counsel wishes to ask questions? Examined by Mr. Krgovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Stanimirovic.

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My name is Dragan Krgovic. I'm one of the Defence counsel of Mr. Miroslav Tadic. In view of the fact that in your replies to my colleague's questions, you touched upon some issues that concerned the defence of my client, I will put a few questions to you on that topic. When my colleague Mr. Pantelic asked you about your work and showed you a document, you said that you had also been engaged in civilian protection tasks. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As I understand it, you were a member of the civilian protection staff. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were in this post before, during, and after the outbreak of hostilities in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what your role was in civilian protection? Was it to prepare teams according to areas of town? Was it in training or something else?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My role was to look after refugees when they arrived in Samac. This happened on several occasions, a hundred, two hundred, or three hundred people would turn up all at once. And I also had a very serious task which I myself set up, and that was to train first-aid teams. I selected people from various parts of town, people who would come to the health centre. They would complete the course of training, receive equipment and material, and go home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you trained first-aid teams by various parts of town, and this was part of your work in the civilian protection?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you refer to refugees, I assume you mean receiving them and giving them first aid, or whatever medical treatment was immediately required. I presume this was your role.

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was one of our roles. We gave assistance to all refugees, not just those who were exchanged --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: There was some misunderstanding. I believe that the interpreters didn't catch the question that my colleague posed. He was talking about people who were coming from the exchanges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krgovic can repeat the question, I hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you spoke of the people who arrived and received first aid, you also mentioned people who had been exchanged; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you did this as part of the civilian protection; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was engaged both in the civilian protection and in the civilian health centre, so it's hard for me to say what role I was performing at any given time. You could say, however --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you were doing this in cooperation with the civilian protection?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. I was a member of the civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Stanimirovic. I have finished my examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The Defence of Mr. Zaric does not wish to examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examination, Mr. Weiner. Cross-examined by Mr. Weiner:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Stanimirovic. My name is Phillip Weiner and I'm going to ask you some questions on behalf of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm still a little confused about some testimony you gave just a few moments ago and which Judge Williams asked you about hiding people. Why would you be hiding people. You said to help them. Who are you hiding these people from? Could you please explain that?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the first day of the war, if we call it that, we had a colleague among us who was a Muslim. In the evening, when we found out that the Serbs were in town, she asked that we admit her parents to hospital because she thought that in hospital they would be safer than they would be if they stayed at home, and we did this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you do that at any other times during the war? When you said you hid people, was that the only occasion or were there other times that you hid non-Serb civilians in that hospital?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were other occasions. I can't remember all the names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you indicated that when you needed money, oil, supplies, you called your good friend Dr. Simic. Do you agree that he was in a powerful position in the municipality, so he was able to help you?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with what you say, that he was an influential man, because he protected me and I was able to do what I did. For a time, he was the chief, or the president, of the board of management of the health centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you aware that he was also the president of both the Crisis Staff and War Presidency of the Serbian municipality of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, there are the authorities, the Crisis Staff, as you call it, they were the authorities, or the municipal people, as we referred to them, and he was one of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was in this -- these authorities, on this Crisis Staff, and were you aware that he was actually the president of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that when he gave me his support as the president of the board of management of the health centre, that I would be able to organise the service in any way I wanted, and he told me to organise it properly and that I would not have any problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if you wanted to get something done, you went to him; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. This question is rather general. If I may. What does that mean, something done? My learned friend should be more specific with this kind of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you wanted to get a project organised, if you needed materials, you went to him and he would get it done; correct? You have to say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You mean within the medical services?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He would take care of it for you? You're nodding yes; is that correct? You're nodding your head up and down. Does that mean yes or ...?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is quite correct. I said when I wanted to organise vaccination, he gave me the funds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you also indicated that you organised an infirmary at the TO, or the Territorial Defence building. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Outpatients clinic. An outpatients clinic. That is an institution where patients come in. They finish their work and then they leave. They don't stay in bed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I understand that. They weren't allowed to leave the Territorial Defence building. They were prisoners. So you -- where in the Territorial Defence building was this outpatient clinic?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I said that I was fortunate enough not to have to test my possibilities, because had anyone needed hospital care, I would have had to take him to hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no. Where within the Territorial Defence building was this clinic? Where was it located? In the yard, in the front office where the guards slept? Where within the building?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a special room in which I set up the outpatients' clinic, because I didn't like the guards hearing what I was talking about with my patients.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, while you were in this room, persons were brought to you. You didn't go into each of the rooms where prisoners were held and examine prisons. Persons -- prisoners were brought to you; correct?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And while you were there, approximately how many times did you go to the TO, to this clinic? How many times?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once a week. That was mandatory. But if there was a lot to do, I would come in twice a week. Now you're putting me in an uncomfortable situation, you know, because there were some friends of mine in that prison whose wives were at liberty. And one could say that I was helping them to communicate, and that was not a good thing to be known about someone at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you did testify that you had a duty and obligation as a physician to go there and help these people, so there's no problem that you went there and passed messages or food. My question to you is: How long of a period? You said you started sometime in the fall and then it stopped some time later because the prisoners were moved out. So did you go for about two months, three months? That's what I'm looking for.

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was two months, but I can't be certain. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, during this two months, did you ever go in and inspect the rooms were the prisoners were being held or did you stay in your clinic area?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed in my clinic area. I didn't visit the rooms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So basically, you're not really familiar with the sanitation conditions inside those rooms where the prisons were being held.

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
