utterances.text: And you're not familiar with the bedding or blankets that were available, if any, in those rooms; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's go across the street to the SUP, or the police station. Did you have a clinic in the police station too?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where within the police station or SUP did you have that clinic?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a room which had not been really set aside on purpose as a clinic, but whenever I arrived, I was allowed to use it. And it was right across two other rooms, where the prisoners were held.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you ever go or enter the rooms which were -- the various rooms in the police station, in the garage area, where prisoners were being held and inspect them? Did you ever inspect any of those detention rooms at the police station or in the garage area behind the police station?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't able to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever inspect any of the rooms in the basement or the cellar of that police station, where prisoners had been held at various times?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't able to do that either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And obviously, since you hadn't been in there, you're not aware of any sanitation facilities that they had within these rooms.

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're not aware as to the number of persons that were being held in any of these rooms or the garages behind the police station?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during the fall of 1992, do you remember while you were at the police station treating or meeting with a prisoner Izet Ramusovic? Do you remember that particular situation? I know you must have dealt with thousands of patients over the past 20 years, but do you recall, is it Ramusovic?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should remember him, because it rings a bell. If I could see a photograph, I'm sure I would remember him. I'm much better at remembering faces than I am at remembering names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe I can help you. When you were meeting with him or treating him, he had a broken nose, a bruised jaw, bruises on his body. He had some teeth that had been extracted against his will by some guards, pulled some of his teeth. Does that refresh your recollection about meeting with Izet Ramusovic, or Ramusovic?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If what you say is correct, they wouldn't have brought a patient like that to me, certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So are you saying if a prisoner was beaten, the guards would have hid him as opposed to bring him to you?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said. I said that I had no patients of that kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, sir, are you aware that prior to your setting up infirmaries at the SUP and the TO in Zasavica, the isolation area which you mentioned, are you aware that other doctors from your staff, such as Dr. Jusufovic, Dr. Ruza Masic, Dr. Zorka Hadzialiagic, Dr. Nogic, Dr. Hasinovic [phoen], were also visiting prisoners at the various prison camps throughout Bosanski Samac? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that, because as soon as I arrived in Samac, they told me that. And then to spare them any possible unpleasantness they might have had, I went.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they tell you about the conditions at the Territorial Defence building, the police station, the primary school, and the high school, the conditions of the facilities, as well as the conditions of the prisoners, that they had been visiting all spring and summer long? Did you have that discussion with them?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They told me some things, and then I attempted -- or I endeavoured to have the clinic set up and to have the prisoners take baths, without fail, and that they be allowed to change their underwear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they told you, then, I have to assume, and could you answer, that the prisoners were wearing dirty clothes, they weren't able to bathe? Did they describe the -- you nod your head in a position of up and down, which means yes?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They told me that, and I made an effort to improve things. I mentioned my role in the Red Cross and the Geneva Conventions. Although I know that 80 per cent of the people who were there don't even know where Geneva is, let alone what the Geneva Conventions are about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, just a couple of things, sir, before we get into the Geneva Conventions. For the record, everything you say and what I say is typed in, so you can't nod your head up and down or sideways. You have to say yes or no. But they told you about the poor sanitation conditions there, and you tried to help; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they also tell you about the very poor nutrition system that was occurring there, the meals that these people were getting, or if you want to call it how these people were being starved? Did they tell you that?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they tell you that the prisoners were receiving one meal a day consisting of one slice of bread, a teaspoon of either lard or jam, and a cup of tea, obviously not a nutritious meal for an adult male? Did they tell you that, sir?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My colleagues didn't tell me about that, but examining the patients in the clinic I opened there, because there were some friends of mine there, they told me that themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So by the fall, you were aware of the poor sanitary conditions, lack of clean clothes, and poor food, or starving, if you want to call it, of the prisoners. You were aware of those three things; correct? That's your testimony.

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did those doctors also tell you about their visits during the spring and summer and dealt with prisoners that were beaten and bruised and bloodied? Did they tell you that?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't tell me that. I think they were afraid to tell me, though I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, but you've since learned, either from your friends and your -- people you treated in the fall, or later, that horrible things happened at these camps?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard from my friends about some things we could call very bad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Such as beatings and torture and murder?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about the beatings. As for the other things, I didn't hear that, because it's very hard still for people to talk about it. I'll probably hear about it later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did these doctors, and it's several of them, local doctors that were going to the prisoners, did they ever say that Dr. Simic, the defendant here, Dr. Simic, accompanied them to any of these prison camps or prisons and treated the prisoners? Did any of them tell you that?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody told me that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see Dr. Simic at the Territorial Defence building or the police station treating prisoners?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Dr. Simic ever go with you to the Territorial Defence building or to the police station and assist you in treating prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: This is actually the very same question that was posed at this moment. If he didn't see Mr. Simic, how could he go together with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No. One is did he see him there. Another one is: Did he accompany him, is the second question, whether or not he accompanied him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lazarevic, it means that he had accompanied him, he would have seen him. Anyway, ask your question. I can see where you're trying to get.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Dr. Simic ever accompany you to the TO building or to the police station to treat prisoners?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, did Dr. Simic ever either accompany you or did you see Dr. Simic at the -- at Zasavica, which you described as the isolation camp or the isolation place? Did you see Dr. Simic there treating prisoners or did he accompany you there to treat prisoners or isolated persons, how you want to describe them?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I neither saw him, nor did he go with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just a couple of issues. Re-examined by Mr. Pantelic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor has just asked you about the persons in the hospital, and that was also a question of Her Honour Judge Williams. Tell me: Were there any Serbs who sought shelter in the hospital in order to avoid something or things like that?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Conditionally, there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us be more precise. What does this conditionally mean? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: His question is: Were Serbs -- were there Serbs in the hospital seeking shelter. Our question concerned whether or not people were being hidden. Two different things. Anyone can go to a school, a police station, any local building to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It may mean the same thing really. Seeking shelter may also mean, you know, asking to be hidden there. Maybe it's a matter of language.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Language.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So let me repeat. I asked you: Were there any Serbs who were hiding in the medical centre?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I do know, those were the soldiers who didn't want to go to the front line. Then they got sick, stayed in the hospital bed for five or six days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then the Prosecutor went on to ask you about the relationship with the civilian authorities. This needs to be clarified, and I will be very specific. What was the role of the municipal Executive Council, the secretariat for agriculture, the secretariat for social welfare? What was -- were -- was your relationship with these specific departments within the municipality?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not very versatile in the organisation of municipal authorities. I have a general term for them: Councillors or authorities. I did not know who among them did -- what specific job they did. I learned about that after Mr. Simic had left Samac. After that, I saw who was doing what there, but I wasn't interested any longer. That was already after 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Stanimirovic. Let us be precise about certain things and let us help the Chamber about that. What I would like to know is: Do you know who was the president of the Executive Council at the time when you took the post of the director of the health centre? Do you know his name?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you -- did you personally know Milan Simic?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know what his function was?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next question that I would like to ask you relates to the line of questioning of the Prosecutor. When you contacted the detainees in the outpatient clinics that you described, had any among them decidedly and explicitly complained to you about medical services?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Decidedly, they didn't, because one never knows when he -- one may say the truth or when one must not tell the truth. What do you think how it would be if somebody was listening in on the other side of the door how this person would end up?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your engagement in setting up these clinics, how do you estimate whether there was any change in the quality of services rendered?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came to Samac, I think that is what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described the relationship with Stevan Todorovic, and this is connected with the previous question, so let me ask you this: Did you contact Stevan Todorovic and insist that these conditions that you had tried to improve, that they may be maintained at the level that you had set up?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I explained to him that he might also fall sick and that he should allow that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Sorry. Excuse me, Mr. Pantelic. Before you move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Your question on page 51 lines 19 and 20 where you say to the witness: "Your engagement in setting up these clinics, how do you estimate whether there was any change in the quality of services rendered?" I'm uncertain as to what you meant, if that's a fair translation of your question. Change from when to when? And then the answer by the witness: "When I came to Samac, I think that is what happened."

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I don't really understand the question or the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's not -- it's not so clear. Well, my question was very simple, comparing to the situation that was prior to his engagement. And then during the period when he was engaged, how he can describe it in terms of quality. But I will ask again this question, because obviously the answer is not so clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: So if I understand you now correctly, what you're going to be asking is whether the quality in medical services was the same during the war period at these two outpatient clinics, whether it was the same as the quality of medical services before the war; is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In fact, during the war, but there are two periods: When he was in charge and when he was not. That's the particular period which I would like to know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Dr. Stanimirovic, A: How would you describe the situation in these outpatient clinics that you had established in September 1992? According to your professional standards, was that an acceptable situation, what you have organised? That's what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The very thought that you, as a detainee, and if you have some health problems, must report this to a guard who is a completely incompetent person, and he is to decide whether he was going to call a doctor or not, is sufficient reason for those people to feel insecure. So when I open an outpatient clinic and I say that, for example, every Tuesday, I will be there at 10.00, and I stick to this, then that is a real improvement, especially since I know how many people wanted to be examined and asked for examination. And if you had ten such people and they tell me that there were only five, among those five, somebody will definitely tell me that there were another five who were not allowed to be examined. Then I will ask for them to be brought for examination. This did not happen, but there was a possibility for such a situation to occur.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You answered to the Prosecutor's question, who mentioned a number of your female and male colleagues who, in the period before you had set up these medical services, had rendered medical services to the people in detention. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In September, you have raised this -- you have raised this to a higher level. So what I'm interested at this point is whether these same colleagues of yours, who in the previous period rendered these services at times, participate in your organisation of medical services which you initiated in September 1992.

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not participate in the work concerning the outpatients hospitals in the prison, because they would have found it more difficult than it was for me. In that manner, I tried to facilitate the works of my colleagues so that they wouldn't have to go there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So where were they working, then?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They worked at the health centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next line of questioning made by the Prosecutor related to the presence of Dr. Simic and his involvement in these medical functions that you described. Answer me, Dr. Stanimirovic: Did you ever call Dr. Simic to accompany you and to come with you and render these medical services in the clinics that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't, because it wasn't necessary at the time. We had sufficient number of staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Dr. Stanimirovic: Had Dr. Simic ever directly refused any help concerning to medical project or medical services in Samac?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've got no problem with this line of questioning. These are all leading questions, one after another. He can do this in another way that's not as leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'll take care about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Dr. Stanimirovic, will you tell me what knowledge do you have of the involvement of Dr. Simic, with the objective of the better functioning of the medical service in Samac on the whole? Concretely, specifically, do you have any personal knowledge?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've mentioned, he was the chairman of the board of management of the medical centre, of the health centre, so that he also gave me free rein for me to do everything which I considered necessary, and he also told me that if I were ever to be in a situation which was uncomfortable, that he would help me protect myself, because health care was our joint problem and it would indeed have been a disgrace for that system not to have functioned properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, my last question: How would you describe the period from 1992 to 1993, which is the period covered in this particular case? How would you describe the involvement of Dr. Blagoje Simic with a view to the organising of the medical service there and supporting your ideas as the person in charge of these medical institutions in Samac? Please be brief.

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was sufficient for me that he had given me the money for the vaccines, and he told me he would always back me and I was to proceed in the best way I saw possible. I needed no other help, because the colleagues who had remained with me in Samac were highly professional people and people of integrity, very decent people, until the last day, and I say this because some of them had left. So when I try to draw some parallels in my line of work, namely, between then and, for instance, today, I can really say that it has been a pleasure for me to have worked with such people and under such circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Stanimirovic. I've finished with my examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Stanimirovic, for giving evidence to the Tribunal. You are now finished and you may leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I do hope that I have been of assistance to you in your quest for the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In the meantime, Your Honours -- we don't have Mr. Usher here. I have this bundle of documents for the next witness. Three copies for Trial Chamber and two for the Court management team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, and please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Please sit down. Mr. Pantelic, examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Pantelic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness. Will you introduce yourself to the Court.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm Veselin Blagojevic, from Samac. I avail myself of this opportunity to apologise to the Court for having appeared in this attire, sports attire, and this is because my suitcase was lost, and it is still at the airport, I presume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That's all right, Mr. Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is quite understandable. This happens. Things like that will happen, and no one is going to take offence because of that. I do hope that you will be able to recover your baggage soon. But if you do have any problem in relation to that, the basic necessities, of course you can get in touch with the witness unit and they will deal with your problem. Mr. Blagojevic, will you please tell me when and where were you born?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 6th of February, 1953, in the village of Gornja Slatina, near Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a suggestion: After my question, because we are speaking the same language, please make a pause of several seconds so as to allow the interpreters to translate your words and mine into the official language of the Tribunal. Thank you. So will you please tell me where your parents were born, your grandparents, grandmother, grandfather, and since when has your family been living in that area?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: My parents, my forefathers, my grandfathers, were born near Samac, in the village of Slatina, in the village of Gornja Slatina. The generations which we know were actually people who had settled there a long time ago and that mainly engaged in agriculture, farmers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you describe your family situation or marital status, rather? Are you married? Do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I am married. My wife's name is Gordana. I have two children, two sons. The name of the first one is Bojan. He was born in 1983 and he studies electrical engineering. The second son is Ognjen. He was born in 1985 and he goes to secondary school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you personally, do you live in the territory of -- have you been living in the territory of Samac municipality since you were born or have you left it at some time or other and then returned to it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I live in Samac. I was born near Samac and now I reside at Samac. I completed primary school in the village of Tisina and the town of Samac. I completed secondary school in Samac. I left Samac related to doing my military service, which I did from 1972 to 1974. Then I worked in Samac whilst a secondary school pupil, in the factory of building materials. Then in 1976 I left to study at the university in Zagreb. I studied political sciences there, having graduated from the university, I returned to Samac and I found employment in a school as a teacher, as a professor. I taught sociology, as well as defence and protection, in the secondary school. I worked in the school for a year. After that I found other employment also in Samac, in a construction company, which in fact was the legal successor of my previous firm, previous company, and there I worked until 1989, at which time I established my own business in the same line of activity, that is to say, construction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we can say that you have quite an impressive experience in construction and building, in this branch, since you worked in the firms dealing in this particular activity and you yourself have a business and still are in charge of your own private business, dealing in building; is that true?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. After the war, I registered my private firm, which deals in trade of building material and the construction of structures, and this is what I am still doing now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Another thing in your professional career: In the period from 1992, you were first mobilised, were you not, and then you were in a unit for a couple of months. So how long did that last?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the beginning of the war, in view of the fact that I had a war duty station scheduled, I went to this war unit, and I'm a reserve officer by rank. So I stayed in this war unit stationed in the village of Batkusa, from the beginning of the war until I was wounded, and I held the post of assistant commander of the battalion i.e., detachment. On the 17th of August, I was wounded in the village of Batkusa. I was wounded at a time when we were replacing men on the front line. After I had gone to hospital and recovered and after I had spent some time on sick leave, I was given the post of secretary for housing and municipal affairs, which is to say I was assigned to work as part of my work obligation, work duty, I was assigned to work there as part of my work duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I suppose this was the municipal administration where you acted as secretary for housing and municipal affairs?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I'm not objecting, but there is a portion of the evidence where the witness refers to his being in a unit and reporting to that unit. You have no idea what unit that is, if it has a name, designation, anything like that. It might be useful for you to have that, so that you know what the witness is talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have no problem to clarify, if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Blagojevic, please tell us: So you had this war duty station, you were mobilised as a reserve officer into a unit. Which unit? Will you give me a precise definition, description, rather, of that unit.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: The unit to which I've been assigned was called the 1st Detachment. It was of the rank of a battalion. And I was the assistant commander of that battalion, assistant battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the Superior Command structure there? Was the detachment a composite part of a wider combat unit, of a wider military unit?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: The battalion, or the detachment to which I belonged, was a part of the establishment structure of the 17th Tactical Group i.e., later of the 2nd Posavina Brigade of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell me where the seat -- the command was of the 1st Detachment?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: The HQ of the 1st detachment was in the village of Batkusa, near Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us revert to a period in your -- to a specific period in your professional life, when you worked in the construction company called Gradnja, in Samac. Will you tell us what particular department you were in charge of and what was your work about within that particular department, from 1981 to 1985, in this civil engineer -- in construction company called Gradnja?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: As I said, I completed the faculty of political sciences and worked as a professor of sociology, and defence and protection. In the construction company in which I found employment, I was in charge of what was called defensive preparation of the enterprise, namely, work related to the preparation of the enterprise for operation in extraordinary war conditions. That is the work I did until 1985, in other words. And after that, I was appointed as a director of one sector of that enterprise, in which there were about -- or rather, between 20 and 25 people, and this sector did commercial accounting and financial work for the production segments of the enterprise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What could be of interest and of relevance to this process is precisely your experience in doing this work of the transition of the enterprise to operation in a state of war and the defensive preparations of the enterprise. So can you explain in a couple of words what that implied, and on the basis of what regulations was an enterprise duty-bound to prepare itself for operating in war conditions? What did this look like? What did you actually do and what were the regulations relevant to this?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: There was a series of regulations governing this particular subject-matter and binding all state-owned enterprises to undertake defensive preparations, i.e., to undertake detailed planning and preparations of their enterprise for operation in conditions of war and in situations of war. This primarily was based on the law on total National Defence, the civilian protection law, and a series of other subsidiary pieces of legislation, so that all state-owned enterprises were under the obligation to undertake preparations to prepare their enterprises for their enterprises to be able to continue operations in war conditions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the period between October 1991 until the end of December 1993, were you a member of any party?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I was not a member of any party during that period. I had been a member of the League of Communists from 1975 to, say, 1988, at which time the Communist Party, namely League of Communists of Yugoslavia and of Bosnia-Herzegovina mainly lost its raison d'etre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe what you personally know about the period between October 1991 until mid-April 1992 in the sense of the inter-ethnic atmosphere which obtained in the city in which you lived, which is in Samac? What did you notice? What are your personal experiences and observations in regard to that particular period?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in a few words, it was very unpleasant to live in Samac, and probably in Bosnia-Herzegovina, for the majority of citizens. This was mainly the period when political parties were established that used such symbols that they revoked memories of past -- bad past times. I remember some details when the SDA party was established in Samac, when a great many people, with lots of noise and shouting, came to this rally, and that was practically a demonstration of crude force and the wakening up or the revocation of some bad old memories. The similar situation occurred when the HDZ was formed. Perhaps that is how probably Croats and Muslims perceived the establishment of the SDS, which was a third nationalist party in Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How would you describe that? Was that national or nationalistic?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Those were national parties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: Since at the time you were not a member of any political party, what were your observations as a resident, as a citizen of that town, in shops, in restaurants, on the streets? Can you tell us what was your personal perception of that time? Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: People were mostly, at the very beginning, when these things started to happen, people tried to preserve their usual order of things. However, despite that, a gradual separation and segregation set in. There were cafes where Muslims would congregate where Croats would get together, and mainly the culmination of fear and fright from war occurred when, in the Serbian village of Sijekovac, near Brod --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I have to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We shall take our break and resume our proceedings at 1805.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic. You are continuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Blagojevic, before the break, you started to explain your personal knowledge about the atmosphere that prevailed in Samac itself. You mentioned that there was division along ethnic lines, that members of all three ethnic communities started to separate into their own communities. Tell me: Do you know of any incidents that happened in late 1992 until April 1993 in Samac?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: There were a few incidents that I remember. One of them I think happened in winter 1991/1992, when two men who, let's say, were in favour of Yugoslavia, one of them was a Muslim and the other one I think was a Serb, were wounded by armed SDA extremists. And a very interesting case -- or rather, an incident, I think happened somewhat earlier, when a young man, a Muslim, in a cafe called Valentino, clumsily activated a hand grenade. He was killed on that occasion and a Serbian girl was wounded. I think that was his girlfriend. This incident, the leadership of the SDA in Samac used for political purposes, and more or less they informed their own public, so to say, that that was done by the Serbs, and many Muslim residents of Samac were ready to carry out a pogrom of Serbs. However, when they -- when some of those people learned the real truth, the situation calmed down. But those were two significant and rather unpleasant incidents carved in my memory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your personal knowledge, if you have any, concerning the arming and the increased presence of armed civilians in the period late 1991 and April 1992 in Samac? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Regardless of one's profession, and I repeat, I had my own private business, it wasn't able for anyone to live in Samac and not listen to, or rather, involuntarily hear some unpleasant news. Specifically, in my neighbourhood, Muslims were armed in the building of the power supply company, and that was organised by a certain Mr. Trnaro [phoen], who was one among the top people of the indiscernible Samac and also by Mr. Huskic, Mr. Izetbegovic, and some other people whose names I cannot remember at this moment. The same situation was with the arming of Croats. Mainly it happened that someone boasted to have given a substantial amount of money for weapons to be procured. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, just to -- a clarification in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Sorry. Just bear with me, please. Yes. Line 23 of page 64, or thereabouts, there's a reference to a certain Mr. Trnaro, who was one among the top people of the "something" Samac. I thought the witness might have referred to the SDA and I just want to make sure it's clear, if indeed it was a reference to the SDA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic can clear that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I am grateful to my learned friend. I will clarify that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since there was a mistake in the transcript, you mentioned that in your neighbourhood, Muslims were being armed within the waterworks or something like that and that somebody had organised this. Could you repeat this portion? What did you say? Who was the organiser? Who was the person and what was his role in the structure, political party structure in Samac or any other structure? Can you clarify that, please?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: A certain Mr. Huskic, Mr. Coner, that was in fact his nickname, then Izetbegovic, and a few other people whose names I cannot remember now, but I know that there were quite a few of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that this Mr. Coner was something in some organisation. What did you refer to, in a Samac organisation? What did you refer to?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: He was, politically speaking, in the leadership of the Samac SDA, and I don't know which specific position he held, but he was employed with the waterworks and probably that was rather convenient circumstances for this operation to be done covertly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1991 and 1992, you had your private business and probably you went on business trips. Did you notice anything unusual that you recall during those trips and that you can tell us now?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I remember a few details during some of my trips, and those were not pleasant details. Once, I think that was in late 1991, I was returning from Zivinice. That is a small town near Tuzla and some 80 kilometres from Samac. I was travelling during the night, and I was stopped by armed patrols. In most of the villages that I passed through, they mainly wanted to see my documents, and as soon as they saw my name, then they searched my car. On the road between Zivinice and Tuzla, there are a few small Serbian villages, and nobody stopped me there. The second situation that took place approximately at the same time was when I was returning from Orasje, and some 20 kilometres from Samac, where mostly Croats live, in the village of Domaljevac, I was stopped by an armed patrol. However, I did not have problems at that occasion because I was stopped by one of my students, who just bade me good night as his teacher. That was a very nice epilogue to this story. But it was rather unpleasant to be stopped by armed men in the middle of the night. Also, another situation was when I had to go on business to Novi Sad. I set off in the early morning hours from my flat, and I couldn't get out of Samac because the people, young people from the SDA, probably members of some military structures, had blocked Samac. I knew those youngsters very well. I had to leave the town very quickly because I was in a hurry, but that was impossible. That is when I felt hostage in my own town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Blagojevic: When did you practically respond to your military duty, to your war assignment?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I reported to my unit in the Serbian village of Batkusa in the afternoon of the 17th of April. On the day before or, to be precise, I didn't spend the night between the 16th and the 17th of April in Samac. Instead, I spent the night at my parents' place in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't hear the name of the village.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: And my wife and children were in Belgrade, in a safe place. During the night or, more precisely, around 2.00 a.m., I was woken by shots and I heard that there was an armed conflict between the Serbian forces, on the one side, and the Croatian and Muslim on the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The name of the village, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Blagojevic, can you tell us, what is the name of the village where you spent the night with your parents?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: That is the village of Pisari, two kilometres from Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the commander of your unit? I presume that you reported to your war assignment.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: My superior officer was Mr. Mico Ivanovic. He was a detachment commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What in particular was your role and your activity in this detachment from mid-April onwards until you were wounded? What tasks did you perform and what had been happening at the front line?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I was the assistant of the commander of the detachment, and it was my duty to arrange the shifts on the front line, or rather, to be the leader of a shift on the front line. We called it the komandir or shift leader of the line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, none of this material appears in the summary of what this witness is going to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's line 2, Your Honour, on the page 5, that he will testify on the following facts: As a reserve officer of the JNA, he was a member of the 17th Tactical Group, which means including his duties during his assignment. So very briefly -- MR. DI FAZIO: Well, it doesn't say that, and he's already given evidence that he was in the 1st Detachment, which was part of the 17th Tactical Group. There's nothing here about a detailed analysis of events of the night of the 16th and 17th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic. It's the activities of the 16th and 17th which are not included. His membership to the 17th Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Including other factual allegations, Your Honour, if I may, from the indictment, including the alleged takeover and events on 16 or 17 of April. But I'm not going to explore this issue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Because, you see, when you're asked to provide summaries, precisely that's what you do. You don't escape under the overall phrase of other factual allegations. You should have named them in the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It is not of so big importance, you know, his activities in his unit. MR. DI FAZIO: It is. Forcible takeover is one of the main points in the indictment. We're entitled to know about this beforehand so that we can do our research, prepare for our cross-examination, so on. It's a fundamental point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. But, Mr. Pantelic's witness is not discussing that from the summaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Go ahead with the contents of the summaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So until the time you were wounded, I think, in August 1992, you were at the front line. Where was this?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Would you repeat your question, Mr. Pantelic? I didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you up to August 1992, when you were wounded, what part of the front line were you stationed at?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I was at Batkusa, Brnik [phoen], Dreznica, that part of the front line. And there I was shift leader of the line and it was my task, with my shift, to spend a certain time there. Most often, this was a period of 12 hours, in normal circumstances, that is, if there were no combat operations going on actively. If there was action, then we would have to stay at the front line until the operations were over, regardless of whether we had been attacked, whether we had been pushed back, or whether there was sporadic shooting. This happened very often in the beginning of the war because both armies had no war experience, or rather, neither of the armies had any war experience.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you were wounded, what happened?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I was wounded on the 17th of August, in the village of Batkusa, and I was given first aid by Dr. Ozren, who was here before me. After that, I was sent to the brigade infirmary, or clinic, and then to Bijeljina, to be operated on. And my sick leave, or the time I spent in hospital, amounted to about 30 days, after which I was assigned to work duty, although my wounds had still not completely healed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you recollect when you were appointed municipal secretary for utilities and housing?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I think it was around the 12th or 20th of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who informed you of this work obligation? Did you have to report to your military unit? Were they informed of your new assignment? Can you explain the mechanism to us?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I was informed that I had been reassigned to work duty while I was still on sick leave, after I had been wounded. I received this information from the President of the Executive Board, Milan Simic, that I had been assigned to these tasks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe to us what your work consisted in, in these first few weeks after your appointment? What did you find when you arrived at work? What problems did you face in the municipality? Tell us something about this period of time, and then we will pass on to discuss some documents.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: When the military operations began in Bosanski Samac, that is, in our municipality, very many people came from other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina, from the neighbouring municipalities, from Croatia, and there were many people in Samac who had no accommodation. Before I arrived, some of this work was being done by the Red Cross, and a whole village, which was called Srnice, from the municipality of Gradacac, was accommodated in a single day, or rather, they were expelled in a single day, and they were put in the village of Hasici, in a single day. I think this was the largest collective housing of refugees, of people with nowhere to live, up to the time I arrived, and this was done by the secretary for utilities and housing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of these refugees?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: These were Serbs, or rather, the whole village, from the municipality of Gradacac, which was called Srnice. When I took up the post of secretary, a decision was already being prepared on giving housing to people with nowhere to live, on a temporary basis, and all the accompanying documents had already been prepared, such as the register, or rather, a record of the condition in which the building was, the decision on granting these premises for temporary accommodation, the municipal service received more than 500 applications for the allocation of housing for people who had no housing in the area of the municipality. Therefore, pursuant to the decree issued by the Serbian Republic -- the government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the decree on the allocation of housing and business premises, it was possible to begin the planned and organised accommodation of people, and this was my main task.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Within the scope of what municipal organ was your secretariat?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: The secretariat for housing and utilities was an independent organ. That is, it was the organ that implemented these tasks, and it was not part of another body; it was an independent secretariat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please: When you had already taken up your post, did you find any documents, any administrative decisions, or did you start from scratch, so to speak? Can you describe this?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: The Executive Board of the municipality, not the whole board, there was no secretariat, but there was a secretary who had already prepared certain documents, decisions on allocating housing, accompanying documents, such as records, decisions on the allocation of housing, the form of the application for housing. So that certain things had already been prepared, although the secretariat had not yet been set up, and this had to be done, because even before my taking up the post, the problem of finding housing for these people had become very acute.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could we have Exhibit D18/2 to be produced to this witness? I would like to have a discussion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Blagojevic, until we find this document, can you tell us whether you undertook any activities in order to organise the secretariat in accordance with standards and principles of your own, if anything, or did you simply continue the previous practice? Can you explain what you did?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: When I took up the post of secretary, the secretariat had not yet been set up. It was I who set it up. I employed people with experience in housing activities. These were mostly people who were civil engineers or people who before the war had been employed in the housing department or people administering socially owned housing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many employees were there in total in September 1992 in the secretariat, and did this number increase in time?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: In September 1992 there were four of us. Afterwards there were five or six. From time to time some people would arrive, others would leave, but mostly we had about six people working at any given time, after the secretariat had been fully set up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please look at the document before you. I think it has three pages. I assume you are familiar with it, but please have a look.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with this document. It was the law on the basis of which we worked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please put it on the ELMO so that the rest of us can see it as well, the front page, please. When was this decree issued? The document speaks for itself. I see it was published in the Official Gazette in July 1992. So you actually found it and it formed the basis of your work in the secretariat?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Article 2 of this decree, would you please look to the right. I don't know if you can read it on the monitor. If not, you can turn to the right and have a look at it. Article 2 mentions certain buildings and facilities, including housing, residential buildings. Could you please explain what this is about?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to this decree and Article 2, there was a clear definition of what buildings and under what conditions could be allocated for temporary use to persons with no housing, or to homeless persons. This contains a list, which includes catering establishments, tourism establishments, residential, houses and flats, weekend houses or holiday homes, auxiliary premises, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did this look like in practice in Samac from September 1992 until the end of 1993? Were there any criteria that were set up for the allocation of housing? And can you comment on Article 5 of this decree, which is on the second page? Would you explain what this looked like in Samac in practice?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of an application they had submitted, persons who needed temporary accommodation, who had to supply documents along with their application, and depending on whether it was an individual, a single person, or a family, and where they had lived before, they were placed in a certain category. On the basis of this, they were allocated housing that was available at the time. Attempts were made to give housing to people who had come from towns in the town and to people who had lived in villages before, we tried to accommodate them in villages. As for the size of the premises, it depended on the size of the family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Blagojevic, tell me, please, what this looked like in practice. Can you give us a few examples?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's say --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Explain it to us. For example, a person submits an application.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: When an application arrived in the secretariat, depending on how urgent the case was. Let's say it was a person from Central Bosnia who had no friends or people he knew there. Then we responded immediately, because that family was probably staying with a host where they had arrived by chance. And we would allocate temporary housing, a flat or a house that was available to that family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you keep any records on available housing, and who set this up, if there were such records?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: The records I found there when I took up the post of secretary had been drawn up in a very professional manner. I think this was done by a member of the Red Cross. And this documentation, as well as the documentation of the former self-management interest community for housing, which was the former department of housing, and these records were our starting point. In the course of our later work, the secretariat collected information from the field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened if a person had more living space or had a larger house, relative to some of your criteria? Did you undertake any measures in that respect? What was the practice in such a situation in Samac from the time you assumed the post of secretary until the end of 1993? Do you have any examples there?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Although Article 2 provides for the possibility of making available surplus living space to people, we never availed ourselves of that particular possibility until the winter of 1992 and 1993, at which time we were compelled to use that possibility because the winter was very harsh. It was very cold. So that it was inhumane to accommodate people in some deserted village households which mainly were without windows, without fences, and without electricity, electrical power. In such cases, we availed ourselves of the possibility of having flats which were much larger than the family or user in question required, which the family was actually using. We would accommodate other families in such flats. So this winter from 1992 and 1993 was a period when we had very many refugees from the area of Kakanj and Zenica and the Borak Lakes. So that was the time when we mostly applied the provisions of this particular article in this way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: Do you have any knowledge about the actual number of refugees in the territory of Samac municipality towards the end of 1993 -- 1992, sorry.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Towards the end of 1992, there were about 5.000 refugees in the territory of Samac municipality, and these were mostly refugees from the already mentioned village of Srnice, near Orasac, and Serbs from Gradacac and other villages. Many people from Odzak municipality, several people from -- several villages in the vicinity of Zavidovici, Kakanj, and Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: The front line observed to the east from Samac, how did it lie? In which direction? And did the municipality of Samac in 1992 and 1993, was it in the same framework, in the same area? Was it of the same area as prior to April 1993?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Samac municipality --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. So my question was: I want you to compare the territory of Samac municipality from April 1992 until the end of 1993 relatively to its territory, the territory of the municipality of Samac, before April 1992. Because it is written 1993 in the transcript. So please explain that to me.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Samac municipality, from April 1992 until the end of 1993, and thereafter as well, was smaller by several villages than the previous municipality, and some of those villages, the largest ones in Samac municipality, are the villages Domaljevac, Bazik, a part of Grebnice, and the village of Prud, which is on the left bank of the River Sava. Now this village belongs to Odzak municipality. So in 1992, Samac municipality was considerably smaller.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Relative to what area?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Relative to the area of the municipality in the period before the 17th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next thing which I'm interested in is: When a decision was brought in for accommodating refugees in a certain house or apartment, regardless of whether it was deserted or according to the criteria which you applied, could the surplus space could be allocated to other people, was there any obligation on the part of these people to pay any compensation for use of these? Was there any -- was there any obligation on the part of the municipal secretariat to recompense the people living in those flats originally? What was the practice there?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: The decree defined the possibility for compensation for the temporary use of living premises, but we never applied this in Samac, irrespective of to what particular population segment this applied. Actually, it was not applied to anyone, because when the war started, and as the war escalated, the people became increasingly impoverished, so that we assisted that. It would be very inhumane to request compensation from people who are not earning anything or earning very, very little.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me: Do you know anything -- whether after the end of the war this subject-matter of compensation had been dealt with in any way or had there been any such procedures in place, either administrative or judicial ones, if you know, if you have any knowledge of those?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't have any knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me something else: Can you estimate, can you assist on the territory of the entire municipality of Samac, since the time when you assumed the post of secretary of the secretariat, how many decisions and how many particular cases of housing allocation were dealt with successfully in the period until 1993? How many refugee problems did you resolve successfully in that period? Can you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I do not remember the exact number now, but we -- this was a daily routine. This was our daily work, and every day we had -- we resolved a great -- problems of a great number of refugees, refugee families as well as of local people. When I say locals, I mean people from Samac and from the vicinity. Sometimes some of these persons were given accommodation repeatedly, in fact, because their houses were repeatedly damaged. So I believe that in the period 1992 and 1993, we accommodated about five and a half thousand people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any -- were there any collective refugee accommodation arrangements in Samac in this period, until 1993, which is the period relevant to -- covered by the indictment? That is why I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: In the period 1992 to 1993, there were no collective accommodation arrangements, or at least there was no collective arrangement which was of any significant duration, of many days or months, that is. Occasionally, people who came aboard convoys or people from an entire village would come and spend several nights and days in a building, and then they would be resettled. As a rule, they would be allocated a living space in Serbian houses, as a provisional measure, and then we would proceed to provide some more durable accommodation arrangements for them, with flats or houses for their use.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: What was the situation like in the village of Zasavica, in the period when you took up this post until the end of 1993? Who was accommodated there?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: The village of Zasavica was the village which had suffered the least damage from war operations and from shelling, and in that village, apart from the Croats who lived there, were also accommodated people from the vicinity of Zavidovici, concretely speaking, the village of Gostovici. I think that was towards the end of 1992 and in early 1993. This is a very large village, so that the villagers were also accommodated in the area of Modrica municipality. And mainly people were very happy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What nationality -- what ethnicity were these people of?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, the native villagers were Croats. And the people from Gostovici village were Serbs. So the village of Gostovici in the vicinity of Zavidovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, what was the ethnicity of the village -- of the people of the village of Zasavica in the period which you are describing, which is to say autumn 1992 to the end of 1993?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Approximately half of the villagers were Croats who had lived in the village before the war, and the rest were people from Gostovici, the villagers of Gostovici, and several families from the territory of Odzak municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: What was the conditions in Zasavica like, in the sense of the quality of the living conditions? What were the houses made of? What was the environment like? Can you explain the general situation from the construction standpoint?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: The village of Zasavica, as I've already said, was lucky not to have suffered major damage by shelling. It is a nice and wealthy village, with nice, mostly newly built houses. It was a nice -- a pleasant place to live in. There was this person, this man, who was the chairman of the local commune there, a certain Mr. Ivo Pandurevic, who was, we can freely say, a right hand in helping us to accommodate the people who had come from the vicinity of Zavidovici in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you visit the village of Zasavica in an official capacity to inspect the conditions to see what the problems were there? Did you go to see the people there?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I went to Zasavica in my official capacity, on official duty. As a rule, the accommodation of the families there, of any refugee family, had to be organised by the secretariat and the commission for the accommodation of people. We could not have this unfold in an anarchic way with, for instance, a small family occupying a large house or one family occupying a number of flats or housing units. So we had to be there on the spot to take minutes of the actual allocation of the housing unit for temporary use by occupants where we also recorded all the mobile and immobile property on the premises, and thereby, in this way, introduced the new user of the premise in question into -- actually gave him occupancy of the premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's 1900 hours. Is it time for our adjournment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We'll continue our proceedings tomorrow at 1415 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 14th day of January 2003, at 2.15 p.m. 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.00 p.m.,
